svg.title: Growing something small
svg.desc: Original family-manga illustration: plant, related to Growing something small.

text.tspan: To care for a plant is to negotiate a familiar but frequently obscured relationship between intentional design and the contingencies of shared
experience. The question is not whether arrangements are desirable, but what authority they should acquire. A credible position supports
preparation while withholding the assumption that procedural coherence is equivalent to human value.
There is a substantive case for structure: observing a plant helps us respond to what it needs. Here, we check whether the soil feels dry before adding water. The arrangement
earns its legitimacy through the specific difficulty it alleviates, not through its conformity to an abstract ideal of order. Its success is consequently conditional. Once the intervention
demands more attention than the obstacle it removes, the original justification begins to unravel.
An assessment confined to that practical benefit would nevertheless be incomplete, since keeping a simple record helps us learn from changes. In concrete terms, we note which
window gives the plant enough light without scorching its leaves. This introduces a problem of perspective: whose convenience supplies the standard against which improvement is
measured? An apparently neutral procedure may privilege the preferences of its designer. Attentiveness to others makes that asymmetry visible and creates grounds for revision.
What emerges is a qualified defence of planning, rather than a celebration of either control or spontaneity. Arrangements can sustain an experience without exhausting its meaning.
Their authority should remain answerable to the people and circumstances they affect; otherwise, a means of making life more habitable risks becoming the criterion to which life
BUILD YOUR OWN · State a focused main idea. Develop one supporting reason in each body paragraph, with a concrete example. Conclude by connecting the two
reasons without introducing a new argument. Use the structure as a model; write about an experience of your own.
Make a sentence of your own, then answer: What two reasons support the main idea? Explain one example.
